title: Dealing with non-compliant infringers
summary: When takedown notices are ignored, what actually works? Charlie Abrahams weighs law enforcement, litigation, blocking, target analysis and disruption.
body_markdown:
I often read marketing material from online brand and content protection vendors that makes IP rights enforcement sound very straightforward, as if the challenge is all about volume and process.


In some scenarios, given the correct protocols are followed, this can be the case. Using eBay’s VeRO program, or similar offerings from the major legitimate platforms, counterfeit listings can be removed very quickly. Similarly, IP-infringing digital content found on social media sites such as Facebook can be blocked via the platform’s own rights protection technology, which it calls “Content Protection”, or removed in real time via a prescribed process.


In fact, legislation such as the European Union’s Digital Services Act has only encouraged the large-scale platforms to be more compliant, by adding new obligations on top of their safe-harbour protections and setting out very punitive measures for non-compliance, including fines of up to 6% of global turnover.


However, this only represents a proportion of the infringements. During my time in the industry, working across a very large number of clients in different sectors, I would say that around 50% of IP infringements are located either on sources that are totally non-compliant (they consistently and deliberately ignore any form of cease-and-desist process) or on websites owned by non-responsive registrants, where the process to enforce is complex and slow.


Anyone doubting the prevalence of this should just Google “DMCA ignored hosting” to see how large a business this is.


In my opinion, for the biggest rights owners, such as sports leagues, broadcasters, and pharmaceutical, automotive and luxury goods manufacturers, this is one of the most important challenges they face in online brand protection (OBP) today, as this is where the sophisticated infringers, who do the most harm, run their businesses.


A real-life example of the scale of this challenge: despite the huge sums spent by the English Premier League and its broadcasters on anti-piracy solutions, it is still relatively easy to watch pirated Premier League content today.


## Options for dealing with “the other 50%”


There are several ways that rights owners and their agencies have attempted to handle non-compliant sites and hosts.


### Law enforcement


For law enforcement to take any action against a site or platform, a certain amount of data has to be collected so that the digital assets can be traced to human beings against whom action can be taken, along with proof of their non-compliance with legitimate notices. This requires digital and physical investigation work to compile an evidence pack that can be taken to law enforcement, who may or may not take it further, depending on the location and scale of the infringements.


Major brands therefore often hire investigation firms, or use their OBP provider, to compile this information and pass it to law enforcement. In the last few years it has become understood that this sort of criminality is used to fund both organised crime and terrorism, so there has been increasing interest from police forces across much of the Western world, with the FBI, Europol and the City of London Police’s Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit (PIPCU) all running programs against this type of infringer.


This type of action has increased as the profile of online crime has grown, but law enforcement still only has the time and resources to become involved in a tiny proportion of rights infringement issues. So even though it may be effective in some highly visible situations, this path does not really represent a holistic solution to the issue in general.


### Integrating online and offline action


Most of the largest IP owners run physical investigation programs (test purchasing, tracing the source of counterfeits, market and factory raids) as well as OBP, and there is a great opportunity to combine the two to better address non-compliant online infringers.


I sometimes feel that the pendulum has swung from an original emphasis entirely on physical measures to one where a lot of emphasis is put on covering the latest platforms (TikTok, Coupang, Tmall, Flipkart and so on), while it remains a fact that[removing a listing, or even an account, does not by itself get rid of the infringing product](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/the-end-of-takedown-thinking) , which is often just sold via another channel.


Far more effective is to combine online and offline activity so that product can be taken out of circulation, factories closed and, potentially, infringers brought to justice.


What we have also learned is that criminals don’t operate in silos. The same organised groups that were shipping containers of fake handbags through major ports are now also running sophisticated websites, marketplace stores and social media operations. They’ve simply expanded their distribution channels.


I remember working with a major electronics manufacturer that discovered a warehouse raid in Hong Kong, which yielded thousands of counterfeit devices, was directly linked to over 200 online stores across multiple platforms. The physical and digital operations were completely integrated on the criminal side, yet the brand owner was tackling them with two entirely separate programs that barely communicated with each other.


### Litigation


A variation on the above theme is to use the evidence to litigate, either where significant assets reside in a compliant jurisdiction (for example, websites that rely on domains in the .com registry) or against a visible provider that is seen to be involved in multiple infringements.


Over the past 15 years, a number of very high-profile cases have been filed by rights owners in US courts against the owners of vast numbers of sites selling counterfeits (sometimes more than 10,000). One of the first was brought by The North Face against a number of Chinese entities in the Southern District of New York in 2010, resulting in $78m in damages being awarded. More importantly, the brand owners gained the digital assets involved, such as domain names and payment accounts. The large number of these, and the funds seized from those accounts, made the action highly cost-effective and created a template that many others followed, especially in the apparel and luxury goods sectors.


Unfortunately, over time infringers learned to move money more rapidly, and the ability to self-fund this sort of litigation program has largely evaporated, leaving it an expensive and time-consuming path to tread.


In 2018, the Premier League did eventually win its case against Ecatel, a Netherlands-based hosting provider that was found to have been unresponsive to notifications about illegal streaming of sports via its servers. However, the case took years to reach this conclusion. It may have been a moral victory, but by then Ecatel had been dissolved and the same service had moved elsewhere.


In general, litigation has the disadvantages of being costly and slow, and it is more often used to demonstrate that a rights owner is vigorous in defence of their brand than as a truly effective remedy.


### Technology solutions


There are technical means to unilaterally cut off access to sites that are illegally breaching rights. One is blocking access through the collaboration of consumer ISPs, so that the IP addresses of offending services are blocked for a period of time (for example, during the broadcast of a sports event) for any household whose broadband is provided by a participating ISP. This has been used effectively in the UK by both the Premier League and UEFA for digital content, and by Richemont for luxury goods. But it is geographically limited, and costly in terms of getting the blocking order through the courts and agreed by the consumer ISPs.


The other technological solution, specific to digital piracy, is forensic watermarking. It is based on the fact that any illegal broadcast stream originates from an original consumer source, so if you can watermark each individual consumer’s stream, you can find out which one is being illegally rebroadcast and cut it off at source.


This is a costly solution to deploy, as each consumer needs to be uniquely identified, but it works well technically and will be successful if the company deploying it is the sole distributor of the content. However, consider a global sports event or a tier-one movie, which will be licensed to many broadcasters. Unless all of them apply the solution, the pirates are likely to find an unmarked source to distribute, so this is actually far from the “silver bullet” its proponents sometimes claim.


### High-value target analysis


It is now well accepted that much of the serious criminality perpetrated online is carried out by well-organised groups, who run sophisticated businesses using skilled technical and marketing staff, just like any other.


These groups usually drive their sales across many websites, social media profiles, marketplace listings and every other route to market that an e-commerce team would employ. Using a mixture of technology and human analysis, providers are able to tie these online artefacts together and identify the groups that represent “high-value targets”, in the sense that if they could be decommissioned in some way, the impact on the level of infringement would be very significant.


However, while many OBP providers can deliver data about these targets, not all of them have the capability to make it actionable. This is a key reason to integrate online and offline programs, as described above: there are a lot of synergies.


The most effective programs I’ve seen use shared intelligence platforms where both online and offline teams contribute and access information. This might include:


- **Suspect entity databases** with both digital and physical identifiers
- **Geographic heat maps** showing both online seller concentrations and physical seizure locations
- **Timeline tracking** that correlates online activity with physical shipments
- **Financial intelligence** linking payment processors, bank accounts and money flows


### Disruption


One alternative that is gaining favour is “disruption”. It is important to understand that this does not mean some sort of cyber warfare or DDoS attack, where nefarious means are used to harm the infringer’s site.


Rather, it means thinking of the infringer as a business with a brand and a P&L, just like any other competitor. The objective then becomes to damage that brand and increase their cost of operation, so that the business suffers, but only by recourse to legitimate means.


This starts with detailed analysis of the infringer’s value chain: ISPs, hosting providers, technology employed, route to market (where they publicise and sell the illegal service) and payment options. It is then possible to take a number of actions that impair the value chain, for example flagging the illegal activity to relevant providers so that they withdraw their service, or getting the sites marked as suspicious or fraudulent. Consumers using the service then see pop-up warnings, which in turn may cause the infringer to switch services or change some of the technology they have deployed. If this is done often enough, it results in repeated changes to usability and harm to the end-user experience.


Similarly, negative feedback could be posted on the social platforms where the illegal site is advertised, so that doubt is created in the mind of the potential customer and the infringer’s online brand is damaged.


In addition, payment services are a key component of the chain in any business. Identifying the routes a criminal group uses to take payment for illicit content, and then taking steps to get the seller blacklisted by those services or by merchant acquirers, is another path that will impair their viability.


## Where the battle has to be fought


As I mentioned at the start, OBP vendors tend to focus on how easily marketplace listings and illegal content can be removed from legitimate platforms, but this is only part of the problem. As these processes have become slicker, and many suppliers now handle them cost-effectively, the large-scale infringers have moved their businesses to places that are harder to reach and invested in a supply chain built on non-compliance.


This means that, for the more sophisticated rights owners in particular, this is exactly where the battle has to be fought today. I am increasingly convinced that a rights protection program needs to be split in two: “bread and butter” solutions that handle the basic issues at as low a cost as possible, and a separate segment of budget dedicated to the more resilient infringers that are actually doing the most long-term damage.


This requires both a significant portion of budget and executive sponsorship, as none of the remedies outlined above is either simple or cheap. But I now consider it should be a key area of focus for rights owners, once they have the basics in place.


*Charlie Abrahams is an independent online brand protection advisor and a contributing writer for MarqVision. The views in this article are his own, and the client examples come from his career in the industry, not from MarqVision customers.*
